messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 25
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Housekeeper
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by caregiver (childhood)
  pcl5: 44

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Nighttime/Dark: Night-time or waking up in the dark, Tactile (Texture): A specific texture associated with the event, Auditory (Children Crying): Kids crying
  Maladaptive Strategies: Drop Responsibilities: give up important responsibilities to stay safe or avoid triggers, Fantasy Escape: I drift off into a world of my own, Never Alone: make sure never to be alone with another person
  Memory: Overwhelm on Recall: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop, Memory Replay: My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over., Full Sensory Reliving: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once
  Negative Appraisals: Exposed to Others: I feel that others can see what happened to me just by looking at me, Dehumanization: I feel like an object, not like a person, Fear of Harm: You can never know who will harm you
  Threat: Flashbacks: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Caleb is a 25-year-old single man of North American background who works as a housekeeper at a mid-sized hotel. He presented for psychological assessment reporting a PCL-5 score of 44, describing a constellation of symptoms that have been intensifying over the past year and that he now recognises as interfering significantly with his ability to function. The trauma at the centre of his presentation is a history of severe physical abuse perpetrated by his primary caregiver during childhood — a pattern that unfolded across years but that he returns to, again and again, in a cluster of specific, visceral memories: the darkness of the room where it most often happened, the rough texture of the fabric against his skin as he was restrained, and the sounds of younger children crying in adjacent rooms, sounds that told him no one was coming and that he was entirely alone with his abuser.

These three sensory details — darkness, texture, children's distress — have not remained in the past. In Caleb's current life, they arrive without warning and with full force. Working a morning shift, he strips a hotel bed and his hand catches the coarse weave of a particular institutional pillowcase; within seconds he is no longer in a hotel corridor but somewhere else entirely, the memory returning not as a recollection but as a full sensory reliving in which he can feel the weight, smell the room, and hear the sounds as though they are happening now. These intrusions play like a film that loops without his consent, and when they come he reports feeling so overwhelmed by emotion that he has to stop whatever he is doing and brace himself against the nearest wall. It is this quality of the memory — its insistence, its completeness, its refusal to stay historical — that has driven most of what his life has become.

Because the memories arrive through these specific sensory gateways, Caleb has reorganised his daily existence around avoiding them. He has requested only daytime shifts and leaves lights on throughout his apartment at night, sleeping fitfully against a backdrop of lamps and screens; when he wakes in the dark regardless, the disorientation is immediate and the physical reaction — racing heart, cold sweat, a jolt of nausea — arrives before he is fully conscious. He has stopped taking on the heavier cleaning responsibilities at the hotel that require him to enter storage rooms alone, citing vague excuses to supervisors, and he has developed a strict rule that he must never be alone with another person in an enclosed space. This last strategy has quietly eroded his social world: colleagues have stopped inviting him for after-shift drinks, and a brief romantic interest ended when he could not explain why he always needed to meet in crowded, well-lit public places and would not come inside. He drifts, too — when the memories press close and avoidance is not possible, he finds himself floating away from the present moment into an internal world of his own construction, a habit that his supervisor has begun to notice and name as inattentiveness.

What Caleb has not been able to avoid is the way the memories have shaped what he believes about himself and the world. He has come to feel, with a certainty that disturbs him, that others can see what was done to him simply by looking at him — that it is written on his face or his posture in a language everyone but him can read. More pervasively, he has arrived at the conviction that he is not quite a person in the way others are; that he was made into an object by what happened, and that this is what he remains. These appraisals do not stay contained: they make the world feel perpetually legible as dangerous, and he is certain that you can never truly know who will harm you, which means that every unfamiliar face, every enclosed space, every moment of proximity to another person requires monitoring. The hypervigilance that results keeps him scanning constantly, and the scanning keeps his nervous system primed, which means the triggers find him faster and the memories return more readily. His efforts to manage this — the avoidance, the withdrawal, the fantasy escapes — have paradoxically kept the memories fresh and his beliefs about himself unchallenged, because nothing he does ever allows him to learn anything different.

Caleb sought help after his supervisor formally documented his performance as deteriorating. What frightens him most, he said quietly at the end of the intake, is not the memories themselves but the possibility that the person he has become is now permanent.
